To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the symmetry energy of nuclear matter can be probed in heavy-ion reactions through the analysis of isotope ratios of fragments and that the experimentally extracted evolution of the symmetry energies with increasing centrality and excitation energy is mainly due to the decrease of the freeze-out density.

the experimentally extracted evolution of the symmetry coefficient with increasing centrality and excitation energy is mainly due to the decreasing freeze-out density rather then the temperature, and the extracted evolution of the isoscaling coefficient is mainly due to both the decreasing freeze-out temperature and the decreasing freeze-out symmetry energy coefficient.

(i) the symmetry energy of neutron-rich matter formed at freeze-out in heavy-ion collisions decreases with increasing centrality, excitation energy, and temperature, (ii) the decrease in symmetry energy is mainly due to the decrease in freeze-out density rather the increase in temperature.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the evolution of the nuclear symmetry potential in hot neutron-rich matter.
a new approach to extract the nuclear symmetry energy of hot and dense neutron-rich matter from the experimentally observed isoscaling in heavy-ion collisions.
the study of the symmetry energy in heavy-ion reactions, which has important implications for understanding the nuclear equation of state and the properties of neutron stars.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the symmetry energy of neutron-rich matter formed at high temperature and low density is much smaller than the one at saturation density and temperature close to zero.

the isoscaling analyses of heavy-ion collision data have been useful for constraining the nuclear symmetry energy at sub-saturation density, but not for constraining the density dependence of the symmetry energy.
the symmetry energy is a function of density and not temperature.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the symmetry energy at freeze-out density decreases with increasing temperature.
the symmetry energy of neutron-rich matter formed at intermediate energy heavy-ion collisions is found to be lower than the one of cold nuclear matter.

isoscaling analyses of heavy-ion reaction data provide us with a new and unique way to extract the symmetry energy in hot neutron-rich matter, which can be used to test the theoretical models for the nuclear symmetry energy.
The main takeaway from our work is that
one should not interpret the isoscaling results as a direct probe of the symmetry energy in the hot and dense matter produced in heavy-ion reactions.
the symmetry energy of nuclear matter at the freeze-out density can be inferred by analyzing the experimental data of isoscaling.
the isoscaling parameters do not directly probe the temperature dependence of the symmetry energy, but rather the freeze-out density dependence of the nuclear symmetry potential.
